The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong through false sharing.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
md: LOTL hunts are baseline hunts in disguise. The tools are legitimate, so the evidence is never the tool alone: it is the tool used by an account, on a host, at a time, or in a sequence that this environment has not seen before.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
md: Do not average the two grades into one number, and do not let the letter drive the digit. "A5" (a reliable source passing on something improbable) is a perfectly valid and useful grade: it tells the reader to check before acting, whoever sent it.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Writing an intelligence product people act on
md: A good intelligence product states a judgement, says how likely and how sure in standard words, shows the evidence and its grade, tells each reader what to do and by when, admits its gaps, and asks for feedback. Everything else in CTI exists to make that page right.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
md: Default deny, check every request in one place, keep that place small, and assume the attacker has read the code. Most broken access control bugs violate at least one of these four.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: CXL can hold *warm* data because a miss there costs about 2x DRAM. Swap can only hold *cold* data because a miss there costs about 100x to 400x. That is why demotion tries CXL first and swap last.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: The padlock icon means "this connection is encrypted to the named site", not "this site is safe". Phishing sites get valid certificates for their own domains in seconds.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
md: mTLS answers "which service is calling?". It does not answer "is this service allowed to do this?". Authorization (orders may charge, but not refund) is still your application's job, keyed on the verified identity.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Why one transformer should both read and draw images
md: An image is not one token. It is hundreds to thousands of positions in the same context window as the text, and that count grows with the square of the resolution. Every unified design is constrained by this budget.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is not a container. A container shares the host's Linux kernel and is isolated by kernel features (namespaces, which give a process its own view of process ids, mounts and network, and cgroups, control groups that cap its CPU, memory and I/O). A unikernel is a real VM with its own tiny kernel, isolated by hardware virtualization.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
md: Unikernels trade **generality for specialization**: fewer layers, smaller images, faster boots and cheaper calls, paid for with porting work, partial POSIX, no processes, weaker tooling and security that depends entirely on what the libOS implements.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Segments: immutable indexes, a write buffer, tombstones and merges
md: Immutable segments turn random in-place updates into sequential writes plus background rewrites. The price is read amplification: every query touches every segment, and dead rows cost time until a merge removes them.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and tuning verl in practice
md: Colocation means **time-sharing**, not free memory. Training states, rollout weights and KV cache take turns on the same GPUs, and sleep and wake are what make the turns possible. A rollout that sets `gpu_memory_utilization` as if it owned the GPU, or a training engine that never offloads, will run out of memory at the transition, not inside either stage.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
md: In an ST-transformer the dominant cost, spatial attention, scales **linearly** with the number of frames instead of quadratically. That is what lets Genie use spatiotemporal context in the tokenizer, the latent action model and the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Device emulation: the attack surface the guest controls
md: "Only root in the guest can reach this device" is not a mitigation on a multi-tenant host. Every cloud customer is root in their own VM. Score device bugs by what a guest administrator can do.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: A defender's playbook for virtualization, and where to practise
md: The boundary between VMs is code you can shrink, sandbox, patch and watch: device models, exit handlers, management services. Hardware gives you the tools (VMX/SVM, EPT/NPT, IOMMU, SNP/TDX/CCA), but every real escape in this course went through software someone could have removed, confined or updated sooner.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: A VLA is a VLM whose output vocabulary also contains actions. Predicting the robot's next move becomes one more question the model answers, so the whole web-pretrained network is reused for control.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Track usage and perplexity during tokenizer training. A 16,384-entry codebook with perplexity 500 behaves like a much smaller vocabulary and wastes embedding rows in every downstream model.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Inside FLASH_ATTN's forward: from slot_mapping to one kernel call
md: Per layer, a backend does two things in a fixed order: scatter this step's K and V to `slot_mapping`, then run one variable-length kernel that reads every key, old and new, from the paged cache. The metadata (`cu_seqlens_q`, `seqused_k`, `block_table`) is the whole contract between them.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
md: A VLM in the LLaVA style is just a language model whose input sequence contains extra tokens that came from an image. Every visual token costs context length and compute exactly like a text token.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
md: Treat a VLM as a strong but fallible reader: give it legible pixels, ask for fields it can copy rather than compute, and verify with rules the document itself provides.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Why learn the weather from 80 years of reanalysis
md: A common misconception is that these models learn from raw observations. They learn to imitate ERA5, so they inherit its biases (GraphCast excludes precipitation from its headline evaluation because ERA5 precipitation has known biases), and they start each forecast from an NWP analysis.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: The intercepting proxy: Burp Suite and ZAP as a workflow
md: A trusted proxy CA in your everyday browser is a standing risk, and a proxy pointed at the wrong host is unauthorised testing. Use a dedicated testing browser, set the target scope before you browse, and turn interception off when you are done.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Blind SSRF, out-of-band checks and server-side browsers
md: OAST proof should stop at the interaction. A DNS lookup or HTTP request to your Collaborator domain proves the fetch; reaching internal services, metadata or credentials on a production target goes beyond proof, and most policies want you to stop and report at that point.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: The same-origin policy: what it blocks and what it lets through
md: The same-origin policy limits what a page can **read** from other origins. It does not stop a page from **sending** requests to them, and it does nothing at all to code that is already running inside your origin. State-changing endpoints need their own protection on the server.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: The map: what happens when you open one file on Windows
md: Windows security is identity attached to processes. A process acts with the token it was given, so "which account ran this, and with which token" is the first question in almost every Windows investigation.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Patch Tuesday and PrintNightmare: closing holes on a schedule
md: Attack surface reduction: every service running as SYSTEM is a door. If a machine does not need a service (printing on a domain controller, SMBv1 anywhere, RDP on the internet), turn it off. You cannot be exploited through code that is not running.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Bluetooth and BLE: pairing, KNOB and BlueBorne
md: Bluetooth has two separate risk classes. Protocol design (pairing models, KNOB's unauthenticated negotiation) decides what a nearby listener or MITM can do to a correct implementation. Implementation bugs (BlueBorne) let a nearby attacker run code, with no pairing at all. Updates fix both; turning Bluetooth off removes the second.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
md: Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
md: WSD separates *making progress* (long constant LR trunk) from *cashing it in* (short cooldown). That separation is what makes checkpoints reusable, runs extendable and scaling studies roughly linear in the number of model sizes instead of quadratic.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices
md: Zero-copy pays when messages are large, the CPU is the bottleneck and the program does not touch the bytes. Any step that reads every byte (software checksums, encryption, hashing, compression) brings the copy back almost for free and erases most of the win.
